newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Steady growth seen for Australian drug firms.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Steady growth seen for Australian drug firms.

text.p: Analysts believe the Australian pharmaceutical sector will continue steady earnings growth in 1997, but expect share market performance to slip for all but selected stocks as investors reconsider cyclical industries.
Analyst Simon Jones of Macquarie Equities told Reuters pharmaceutical stocks in the last couple of years had certainly well outperformed the All Ordinaries index.
"I do not see that happening over the next year or so, mostly because I think it is time for the cyclical stocks to get a look in the Australian market," he said.

Another analyst, who did not want to be named, said the sector had begun to slip in the past three months, due to share price falls in Cortecs International Ltd and Biota Holdings Ltd, the cyclical move, and some nervousness about growth stocks.

The industry features listed companies such as F.H Faulding & Co Ltd, Cortecs and CSL Ltd, privately held Sigma Pharmaceuticals Pty Ltd, and subsidiaries of companies such as Astra AB and Glaxo Wellcome Plc.
The sector also includes a host of biotechnology companies, among them Biota, Norvet Ltd, Cochlear, and Amrad.
Industry figures put estimated 1995/96 pharmaceutical sales in Australia at A$3.5 billion and A$800 million in exports, of which 75 percent are prescription medicines.
Analysts said the pharmaceutical industry was experiencing strong global growth and the Australian industry was no different and well placed strategically.

"We are getting older so we are going to need more medicines and Asia has nothing like the medicines it will need and want and we will get a lot of growth just through exports to Asia," one analyst said.

Analysts welcomed improved exposure to the pharmaceutical wholesaling and distribution sector, through the proposed compliance listing of Australian Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd (API) and a move by Sigma to publicly raise A$55 million.
They said while there was steady double digit growth in wholesaling and distribution, competition was strong and hindering margin growth, so hopes were on Asia.

But the pharmaceutical sector is vulnerable to changes in public policy and regulation. It is awaiting a government response to a review of a scheme that compensates companies for Australia's lower than average drug prices.
The scheme offers payments for investment in research and development, value-added manufacturing and meeting export targets.
Drug producers were also hit by the cut in a research and development tax concession to 125 percent from 150 percent.
One research report has estimated the cut would knock off three to eight percent of net after tax profit forecasts in 1996/97 and 1997/98 for Faulding, CSL and Cochlear Ltd.
At the more speculative end of the sector, biotech stocks were boosted by the recent float of Amrad Corp Ltd, which is seen by analysts as having strong long-term potential.
Biota has entered phase three trials for its influenza treatment which, if approved in the U.S., would give it access to an annual market estimated at up to A$4 billion.
One analyst said Biota could be a "cashbox company", earning a six percent royalty through its development and distribution deal for the treatment with Glaxo Wellcome.
Norvet also is expected to join forces with another multinational to develop its menopausal treatment but, like other biotech stocks, it has been battered recently in the market.

"The problem with (biotech stocks) is the research goes on and on, it takes time and the market often gets a little impatient for news so the shares are more volatile than normal stocks because people get tired of waiting and sell, or think nothing is happening or someone has a better treatment," one analyst said.

Jones said while overseas investors were quite comfortable with biotech stocks, Australian stocks found it difficult to attract risk-averse fund managers here. "The way really to invest in these things is to construct a portfolio: while one goes up, another will come back down," he said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
